content: CD48, also referred to as the Cluster of Differentiation 48 antigen, B-lymphocyte activation marker (BLAST-1), or signaling lymphocytic activation molecule 2 (SLAMF2), is a protein encoded by the CD48 gene in humans. It belongs to the CD2 subfamily of the immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSF), which includes other signaling lymphocyte activation molecule (SLAM) proteins such as CD84, CD150, CD229, and CD244. CD48 is expressed on the surface of lymphocytes, other immune cells, dendritic cells, and endothelial cells, where it plays a role in activation and differentiation pathways. CD48 was the first B-cell-specific cellular differentiation antigen identified in transformed B lymphoblasts. The gene encoding CD48 is located on chromosome 1q23 and consists of four exons. Each exon encodes one of the four domains of CD48: the signal peptide, the variable (V) domain, the constant 2 (C2) domain, and the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor. The cDNA sequence of CD48 contains 1137 nucleotides, encoding a 243-amino acid polypeptide with a molecular weight of approximately 45 kDa. This polypeptide includes a 26-amino acid signal peptide, 194 amino acids corresponding to the mature CD48 protein (comprising the V and C2 domains), and a 23-amino acid C-terminal segment that forms the GPI anchor. The GPI anchor links CD48 to the cell surface via a serine residue at position 220. Notably, CD48 lacks a transmembrane domain and is instead anchored to the cell surface by the GPI linkage, which can be cleaved to release a soluble form of the receptor. CD48 is heavily glycosylated, with five potential asparagine-linked glycosylation sites at positions 40, 44, 104, 162, and 189. Approximately 35-40% of the total molecular weight of CD48 is attributed to its carbohydrate side chains. In terms of interactions, CD48 exhibits a low affinity for CD2, with a dissociation constant (K_D) of 8 μM, which is approximately 5-10 times stronger than other CD2 interactions. CD48 is expressed on all peripheral blood lymphocytes (PBLs), including T cells, B cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and thymocytes. It is also found on the surface of activated T cells, mast cells, monocytes, and granulocytes. However, like other GPI-anchored proteins (GPI-APs), CD48 is absent on erythrocytes (red blood cells). CD48 plays a role in T cell activation by interacting with CD2. This interaction, along with other molecular pairings such as CD28-CD80, TCR-peptide-MHC, and LFA-1-ICAM-1, contributes to the formation of an immunological synapse between T cells and antigen-presenting cells. The CD48-CD2 interaction has been shown to promote lipid raft formation, T cell activation, and the formation of caveolae in macrophages through cell signal transduction mediated by GPI moieties. Clinically, CD48 is being studied as a potential marker in research on inflammation and therapies for conditions such as HIV/AIDS.
